shots.narration: Doug's field guide already has a page for this bird,
and the box marked friend says no.
Doug has decided that was a misunderstanding.
Harmless.
The Boom.
You would think the most dangerous bird alive would announce itself,
and the cassowary does, just not in the way you'd expect.
A study published in two thousand three recorded cassowaries in Papua New Guinea
and found that their booming calls go remarkably low.
The southern cassowary went down to thirty-two hertz,
and its smaller cousin, the dwarf cassowary, went down to twenty-three.
That's right around the lowest key on a piano,
and close to where human hearing starts to give out.
Here's the unsettling part.
You might feel this bird before you hear it.
The lead researcher said that up close, these calls can be heard or felt,
the way people describe standing near rumbling elephants.
So a bird up to two meters tall could be calling a few trees away,
and the first thing you notice might be a rumble in your chest.
The researchers think a voice like this suits an animal that lives alone, spread thinly through dense rainforest.
A deep note can carry through all those leaves to another cassowary a long way off.
Doug felt a buzz in his pocket and checked his phone, but there were no messages.
Three trees back, something tall stopped talking and left.
Doug is fine.
It wasn't calling Doug.
Doug just happened to be standing in the middle of the conversation.
The Helmet.
On top of every cassowary's head sits a tall crest called a casque,
and it looks exactly like something built for headbutting its way through a jungle.
The outside is a sheath of keratin, the same material your hair is made of.
Underneath is a fragile bony core, part honeycomb and part empty space, threaded through with blood vessels.
For around two hundred years, people argued about what it was for.
A shield for ramming through undergrowth, a weapon for fights,
a way to impress a mate, a sound box for the boom.
One major review found its bony core fragile and judged the weapon idea unlikely,
but it still couldn't settle what the thing was actually for.
The surprising answer came in two thousand nineteen.
Researchers pointed thermal cameras at twenty southern cassowaries in weather ranging from five degrees Celsius up to thirty-six,
which is almost exactly the temperature of your own body.
In the cold, the casque let out almost no heat at all,
and in the heat, it let out the most.
The blood vessels inside it can open up to dump heat when the bird is too hot,
and tighten to hold heat in when the air turns cold.
It isn't armour.
It's a radiator.
Doug knocked on it and got nothing back,
so he offered the bird his cap for shade,
then realised it had its own air conditioning.
Doug survived, and we had already sharpened the pencils.
The scariest-looking part of this bird is mostly there to stop it from overheating.
The Plum.
The cassowary is mostly a fruit eater, and it doesn't nibble.
It swallows its fruit whole, often picking it straight up off the forest floor.
One study of southern cassowaries in Australia found them eating the fruit of two hundred and thirty-eight plant species.
In feeding trials, seeds stayed inside the bird for about five hours on average.
That's long enough to carry them a couple of hundred meters, and sometimes more than a kilometer.
The seeds come out undamaged, in a pile of fertiliser, somewhere new.
According to the agency that manages Queensland's Wet Tropics rainforest, more than seventy tree species there have fruit too big for any other forest animal to eat and carry away.
Without the cassowary, those seeds have nobody else to move them.
The strange part is one fruit in particular.
The cassowary plum is a purplish-blue fruit, a little longer than a credit card.
It is one of the southern cassowary's favourite foods, which is exactly how it got its name.
For people, it's toxic.
The bird is the rainforest's gardener, and it can eat the plum.
Doug cannot.
We handed Doug a cassowary plum.
Doug did not agree to this.
He watched the bird swallow one whole,
and did exactly the same thing.
The bird walked off to plant a tree,
and Doug stayed behind as a lesson.
Dangerous.
The Road.
On the roads of far north Queensland, the danger runs the other way,
and it's worth looking at it from the bird's side of the road.
In Australia, cassowaries live only in the far north of Queensland,
and the southern cassowary is listed as Endangered under national law.
Queensland's environment department estimates that there are about four thousand of them left in the wild.
Even that number is soft, because a shy, solitary bird in thick rainforest has always been very hard to count.
The main concert hall at the Sydney Opera House seats up to two thousand six hundred and sixty-four people.
Every wild cassowary in Queensland would fill it,
and there would still be a long queue outside for the second show.
The problem is what happens on the roads.
One study looked at one hundred and ten cassowary deaths with a known cause, between nineteen eighty-six and two thousand four.
Fifty-five percent of those birds were hit by vehicles,
and eighteen percent were killed by dogs.
Queensland's transport department still calls vehicle strikes the leading known cause of cassowary deaths.
The cars are winning.
Roads through their habitat carry yellow cassowary crossing signs,
and one Queensland trial tested warning signs that light up when a driver is going over the limit.
For one item, the dangerous animal on this road is Doug.
Doug saw the sign, braked in plenty of time, and waved.
The cassowary looked at him for a long, long time,
and then it crossed the road.
Nobody died, and on this road that counts as the unusual outcome.
The Quills.
The cassowary can't fly, and most people assume its wings are simply tiny, useless leftovers.
They are tiny, so short that they almost disappear into the body feathers,
but they are a lot stranger than leftovers.
Its body feathers are loose, shaggy and almost hair-like,
because they're missing the tiny hooks that zip a flying bird's feathers together into a smooth surface.
Its feathers even grow as doubles, two shafts of similar length from one base.
Its neck is bright blue, with red wattles hanging down the front,
and in some birds that bare skin even changes colour with mood or excitement.
Then there are the wings themselves.
A study of the southern cassowary's wing found only four long, slightly curved quills,
and some of its flight feathers have stout shafts but no vanes, no barbs, nothing a bird could fly with.
They look like a handful of black knitting needles stuck into a feather duster.
The worst part is what's hidden in there.
The same study found that the second digit of the wing ends in a curved claw.
The bird that can't fly still has a claw on its wing.
Doug stood on a stump and flapped, trying to teach the bird to fly.
It lifted one wing, showed him the quills and the claw, and lowered it.
Doug got the message, climbed down off the stump,
and decided not to bring up flying again.
Even the part of this bird that does nothing has a claw on it.
The Dad.
If you picture a cassowary guarding a nest, you're probably picturing the mother.
You'd be wrong, and in this forest, that's the kind of mistake that matters.
The female lays a clutch of large green eggs,
each one at least as heavy as a full-size soccer ball.
Then she leaves, and she may go on to mate with up to three different males.
From then on, the male takes over completely,
and a female only occasionally steps in, sometimes after the male has died.
He turns the eggs, sits on them for about fifty days,
and rarely eats anything during that whole time,
while the female may already be off starting a family with somebody else.
When the chicks hatch, they're striped in cream and dark brown, which probably helps them vanish into the forest floor.
Within a few days, they follow their father everywhere.
He guards them around the clock and leads them to water and to fruiting trees,
and they stay with him until they're about nine months old, sometimes longer.
Somewhere along the way, between three and six months, the stripes fade and the chicks turn a plain, scruffy brown.
And that's where this becomes dangerous.
The Australian Museum notes that the fathers caring for eggs and chicks are very aggressive during the breeding season.
The angriest parent in this forest is the dad.
Doug saw three small striped birds, crouched down low, and said hi friends.
The friends did not answer, but their father did.
He had barely eaten in fifty days,
and he was not in the mood for visitors.
The Swim.
Most people assume a big, heavy, flightless bird would stay well away from deep water.
It's a reasonable assumption, and Doug made it.
A large cassowary can weigh as much as sixty kilograms,
about the same as six of those big ten-kilogram bags of rice.
Queensland's parks and wildlife service says cassowaries will take to the water to cross from one side of a river to the other,
or to get away from dogs or from a rival cassowary.
The weird part is how far they take it.
In late twenty twenty-three, people at a campground on Bingil Bay in north Queensland
watched something swimming toward the beach from the open sea.
At first they thought it was a turtle, or maybe a shark's fin.
Then a young cassowary walked out of the water and shook itself off.
Officials said they weren't sure how long it had been out there, or why it had gone for a swim.
A young cassowary walking out of the surf at a campground was unusual enough
that Queensland's environment department put out a media release about it.
Doug's escape plan was the river.
For the cassowary, the river is the commute.
Doug jumped in the river and floated on his back, relieved.
Then something that looked a lot like a fin came gliding downstream toward him.
Doug has died. Again.
The cap made it all the way to the coast,
which is more than most swimmers manage.
The Sprint.
Most of the time, a cassowary wanders slowly across the forest floor, head down, picking up fallen fruit.
Standing still, it looks heavy and a little awkward.
That impression doesn't survive seeing one move.
Its legs are long, thick and powerful, covered in tough protective scales, and they end in large, heavy feet.
On them, cassowaries are usually reported at up to fifty kilometers per hour.
That happens to be the default speed limit in built-up areas of Queensland,
so a cassowary running flat out through a quiet street in Cairns would be doing exactly the legal limit.
And, as Doug found out last time, it jumps, too.
But that's not the disturbing part.
That top speed isn't something people describe on an open track.
It's described for a bird running through rainforest, with vines, roots, fallen logs and low branches,
in the kind of place where you can't see more than a few meters ahead.
The Australian Museum says these birds can crash straight through rainforest thickets that look impossible to get through,
and then vanish from view almost at once.
Their tough skin and bristly, hair-like feathers help shield them from the spiny plants that would stop almost anything else.
Thick forest is where Doug is slowest.
It's where the cassowary is fastest.
Doug ran as fast as he could, looked back over his shoulder,
and saw nothing behind him, so he slowed down and relaxed.
Then he looked forward again.
It hadn't been chasing him at all.
It had simply taken the shortcut and gotten there first.
Deadly.
The First Pet.
You would think anyone who had met a cassowary would keep their distance.
People in New Guinea, at least eighteen thousand years ago, seem to have done the opposite.
In twenty twenty-one, a team led by researchers at Penn State studied more than a thousand cassowary eggshell fragments from two rock shelters in New Guinea.
The shells were between eighteen thousand and six thousand years old.
The team worked out how far along each egg had been when someone collected it,
and a large majority had been taken late, when the chicks inside were nearly ready to hatch.
A good number of those late shells showed no burn marks at all.
So the researchers suggest people may have been collecting the eggs on purpose, hatching them, and raising the chicks.
Cassowary chicks imprint on people readily and are easy to raise to full size,
and they are still traded in New Guinea today.
The birds in the rock shelters were most likely dwarf cassowaries,
which grow to around twenty kilograms, about the weight of two big ten-kilogram bags of rice.
That's the small one.
Here comes the part nobody expected.
The team described it as possibly the earliest sign anywhere in the world of people managing the breeding of a bird.
The lead researcher said it came thousands of years before anyone domesticated the chicken.
People may have been raising the most dangerous bird alive since as long as eighteen thousand years ago.
Doug had a weekend.
Doug picked up a chick and said hi friend.
It imprinted on him immediately,
and then it kept on growing.
The people of New Guinea may have had thousands of years of practice,
and Doug skipped all of it.
The Toe.
Every bird alive today is a dinosaur.
Birds sit inside the theropods, the group on the dinosaur family tree that includes the raptors.
They are the only branch of it that made it through the extinction at the end of the age of dinosaurs.
With most birds you would never guess, but the cassowary's feet make it a lot easier.
Each foot has just three toes, because the small first toe that most birds have is simply missing.
The inner one of the three, which anatomists call digit two, carries a long, dagger-like claw.
On a big bird it can reach about ten to twelve centimeters, roughly the length of a long paring-knife blade.
Now look at the raptor dinosaurs, like Deinonychus.
Their famous enlarged killing claw, the one in every museum hall and every dinosaur movie, was also on digit two.
Scientists still argue about how those raptors used theirs,
and the old movie image of slashing is not the favourite answer.
One study compared their feet to those of hawks and eagles,
which hold prey down with an enlarged talon and use their body weight to pin it.
That study suggested the raptor claw was mostly used the same way, to grip prey and keep it there.
Put the two feet side by side, and the unnerving part jumps out.
It's the same toe.
Doug brought a plaster museum cast of a raptor claw,
held it up against the cassowary's foot, and asked whether the two of them matched.
The bird agreed, briefly.
The dinosaurs never really left.
Some of them just gave up hunting and took up fruit.
The Kick.
Guinness World Records and countless headlines call the cassowary the most dangerous bird in the world.
Standing up to two meters tall and weighing as much as sixty kilograms, it certainly looks the part.
A cassowary can kick forward and downward,
and it can jump high enough to strike an adult at chest height.
Those kicks are how a cassowary defends itself against predators.
Its legs end in three toes, and you already know about the inner one.
Here is the part that changes the whole picture.
For all that reputation, only two human deaths are well documented,
and they happened ninety-three years apart.
In nineteen twenty-six, in Queensland, a young hunter struck a cassowary, intending to kill it, and then ran from it and fell.
In two thousand nineteen, in Florida, a man was killed by a cassowary he kept on his own property,
where wildlife officials said he had been breeding the birds.
Fire rescue officials said he had fallen while he was near the bird.
Experts describe cassowaries as naturally shy and wary animals.
Like most animals, they would rather avoid a fight,
and they usually fight only as a last resort, when their own life or their young are threatened.
Conservation scientists point out that people are a much bigger threat to cassowaries than cassowaries have ever been to people.
The most dangerous bird alive has killed two people on record,
and both times, the person had come to the bird.
Once to attack it.
Once to keep it.
Doug read all of that, opened his field guide,
crossed out the word no, and wrote friend, with a question mark.
Then he walked toward the bird.
He came to the bird.
Later that evening, a cassowary found the cap,
looked at it for a while,
and swallowed it whole, like a plum.
Somewhere in this forest, the cap has now been planted.
Doug deaths: one hundred and fifty-four.
The field guide still says no.
Which part of the cassowary would you least like to meet?
Tell us in the comments.
